candidateRows: Worldviews necessarily intertwine metaphysics, ethics, and epistemology while presupposing transcendental conditions that empiricism and scientific method cannot themselves justify.
This establishes the transcendental categories and alleged explanatory deficit that supply the premises for Dyer's subsequent inference to theism.
In his opening case, Dyer describes worldviews and argues that logic, induction, identity, regularity, meaning, and numbers are prior conditions of empirical inquiry.
The Orthodox Christian divine mind grounds universals, truth, natural regularity, and the one-and-many relation, making transcendental categories intelligible.
This is the principal positive inference of the pro case, identifying Orthodox Christian God as the ground required for the disputed transcendental conditions.
Dyer moves from empiricism's alleged inability to justify immaterial invariants to a specifically Orthodox account of universals grounded in God's mind and Logos.
A God-created worldview coherently explains knowledge, dignity, logic, mathematics, ethics, and regularity, whereas materialism or pragmatism leaves them arbitrary.
The comparative claim supplies the exclusivity component of the transcendental argument by alleging that rival materialist accounts cannot ground the same categories.
The closing portion of Dyer's opening contrasts the explanatory resources of Orthodox theism with matter in motion, social construction, and pragmatic use.
Using indispensable presuppositions without knowing an ultimate guarantor is not arbitrary, because practical and philosophical reasons can justify their use.
This rejects the pro argument's claimed dilemma between theistic grounding and arbitrary reliance on logic, truth, dignity, and related presuppositions.
Dyer's claim that relying on transcendental categories without an ultimate theistic justification is arbitrary.
Dillahunty says the opening did not clearly present an argument and distinguishes reasonable reliance on presuppositions from possessing a demonstrable ultimate guarantor.
Belief in God as a guarantor merely assumes the needed foundation, risks circularity, and may misapply physical causality to abstract entities.
The passage directly attacks the proposed bridge from a desire for foundations to God's existence, alleging assumption, circularity, and a category problem about causation.
Dyer's proposal that belief in God provides a genuine explanatory foundation and guarantor for transcendental categories.
Dillahunty grants that belief in a guarantor can make a worldview feel coherent but argues that substituting God for the desired foundation does not establish it.
Logic and a shared external reality are rationally presupposed because of their persistent practical reliability and parsimony, not because certainty is available.
This offers the con side's alternative epistemic basis for logic and shared reality, countering the claim that only a divine guarantor avoids arbitrariness.
Dyer's contention that pragmatic use cannot non-arbitrarily justify logic, induction, or confidence in an external world.
Dillahunty denies access to certainty but argues that logic continually proves reliable in interaction, while a shared reality is more parsimonious than solipsism.
Dyer has not demonstrated the inference from unexplained transcendental categories to God or shown that those categories require an external explanation at all.
This challenges both the validity of the central inference and its explanatory premise, directly contesting whether the transcendental argument establishes the motion.
Dyer's claimed transition from empiricism's unexplained presuppositions to God as their necessary explanatory ground.
Dillahunty argues that the opening listed philosophical issues without supplying a path to God and asks whether truth or logical laws may simply obtain without an external guarantor.
Withholding an unsupported ultimate explanation is intellectually honest, while defining God as explanation-exempt simply relocates rather than resolves the grounding problem.
The argument rebuts the accusation of intellectual bankruptcy and raises a regress or special-exemption objection against God as the terminal explanation.
Dyer's characterization of non-theistic agnosticism about ultimate foundations as intellectual bankruptcy.
Dillahunty says he will not multiply presuppositions merely to secure desired foundations and argues that an explanation needing no explanation is asserted rather than demonstrated.
Transcendental categories are coherent within Orthodox Christianity because a personal God unifies and grounds them, while materialism is self-contradictory.
This is Dyer's direct formulation and clarification of the debated transcendental argument, including the claimed connection between coherence and Orthodox theism.
Dillahunty's objection that the opening supplied no clear argument or demonstrated route from transcendental categories to God.
Dyer expands the category set, distinguishes mind from sense data, invokes coherentism, and identifies the personal Orthodox God as what unifies reality and predication.
The transcendental argument does not infer that reality is purely mental from abstract justification; it seeks a presupposition more fundamental than mathematics.
This clarification protects the central pro inference from an alleged abstraction-to-reality mistake and specifies the deeper level at which the grounding claim operates.
Dillahunty's concern that constructed abstract justifications may not correspond to or guarantee the external world.
Dyer partially concedes the general gap between abstract justification and external reality but denies that his case merely maps the world through a mental or mathematical structure.
A skeptical and pragmatic empiricism cannot justify logic, truth, or induction and therefore lacks coherent grounds for rational debate itself.
The move directly develops the transcendental challenge by arguing that the opposing worldview cannot account for the logical and semantic conditions used in debating.
Matt's skeptical account of justification and his pragmatic reliance on apparently reliable logical practices.

After accepting God as his ultimate presupposition, Jay contrasts that coherentist commitment with Matt's pragmatism and argues that communication, information, logic, and debate require worldview-level grounding.
Rejecting transcendental grounding pushes empiricism toward solipsism, where even acquiring knowledge of solipsism becomes self-undermining.
This supplies the reductio supporting Jay's case that denying the proposed transcendental categories produces destructive epistemic consequences and self-contradiction.
Matt's suggestion that certainty about an external world and other transcendental commitments may remain unavailable.
Jay argues that empiricist doubts about the past, induction, selfhood, and the external world culminate in radical solipsism, which cannot coherently establish its own truth.
Shared logical commitments provide enough common ground for debate without establishing a divine foundation, while adding God imports unsupported explanatory baggage.
The move rejects a core transcendental inference by separating practical agreement about logic from the further claim that logic requires the proposed theistic foundation.
Jay's claim that Matt's worldview cannot justify the common logical and semantic conditions required for debate.

Matt identifies his broadly Humean and foundherentist sympathies, notes that the speakers already share reality and logical rules for discussion, and argues that positing God does not simplify the account.
Fallible presuppositions can support maximal rather than absolute certainty, with confidence proportioned to deductive or inductive support and conclusions remaining revisable.
This gives Matt's positive epistemic alternative to Jay's demand for ultimate justification and explains how rational inquiry can proceed without claims of absolute certainty.
Jay's contention that failure to provide ultimate justification for logic and truth leaves Matt unable to reason or debate coherently.

Matt distinguishes maximal confidence in logical and mathematical conclusions from lower inductive confidence, treats science as tentative and revisable, and says shared reality is sufficient to begin inquiry.
The claim that transcendental categories require a foundation has not been demonstrated, and a coherent explanatory story does not thereby become necessary or true.
The move directly contests the motion's central inference from coherence or explanatory appeal to the necessity and truth of a divine foundation.
Jay's argument that transcendental categories must have a coherent foundation and that God supplies the required justification.
Matt says no foundation has been shown to be required, treats logic's apparent invariance as reasonable evidence, and uses a perfect bridge hand to distinguish a comforting explanation from truth.
Appealing to psychological discomfort is fallacious, while distinguishing levels of certainty itself presupposes truth-bearing categories unavailable on Matt's pragmatic account.
The move answers Matt's positive epistemology by arguing that its own distinctions depend on the very transcendental categories whose grounding is disputed.
Matt's account of maximal certainty and his suggestion that a divine foundation chiefly eases psychological discomfort.
Jay rejects the motivational explanation as an appeal to emotion and argues that Matt cannot distinguish abstract certainty from empirical confidence without presupposing a genuine category of truth.
Transcendental categories are maximally certain because denying them destroys the coherence required for knowledge, predication, science, communication, and practical engagement with reality.
This is a direct affirmative defense of the transcendental argument, connecting the indispensability and mutual dependence of its categories to the proposed divine worldview.
Matt's card-dealing analogy and claim that explanatory coherence neither demonstrates necessity nor establishes the truth of theism.

Jay contrasts ordinary inductive cases with categories indispensable to thought and action, argues that the categories cohere together, and invokes mathematics and engineering as practical manifestations of abstract order.
Coherentism evaluates an interconnected web of beliefs rather than foundational axioms, and allowing Matt's account to stop arbitrarily at logic would equally permit stopping at God.
The move clarifies the affirmative's epistemic framework and charges the opposing account with an arbitrary stopping point at ungrounded logical and metaphysical commitments.
Matt's characterization of coherent truth and his position that logical laws may be accepted without any demonstrated further foundation.

Jay distinguishes a foundational hierarchy from a coherent web connecting logic, identity, God, and ethics, then argues that debate cannot consistently permit an ad hoc assertion that logic simply is.
Treating logical laws as reliable presuppositions is not an arbitrary assertion, whereas adding an undemonstrated foundation merely relocates the presupposition without supporting it.
The move rebuts the alleged parity between presupposing observed logical reliability and presupposing a divine foundation for which no necessity or demonstration has been supplied.
Jay's claim that accepting logical laws without deeper grounding is arbitrary and therefore licenses an equally arbitrary assertion of God.

Matt says he does not assert that logic simply is, but provisionally presupposes its apparent invariance based on continued reliability and sees no reason beyond discomfort to posit an additional foundation.
A successful reductio for theism must establish that an explanation is necessary and eliminate every alternative, neither of which the transcendental argument has accomplished.
The move directly attacks the asserted necessity of theism by identifying missing premises and denying that present explanatory gaps establish the failure of non-theistic alternatives.
Jay's assertion that all reality presupposes God and that non-theistic alternatives reach dead ends sufficient to establish a reductio.

Matt argues that neither the need for an explanation nor the exhaustion of alternatives has been shown, emphasizes that future non-theistic explanations remain possible, and frames uncertainty as a motive for inquiry.
God cannot guarantee the laws of logic because either God can alter them, making them insecure, or cannot alter them and is subject to them.
This dilemma directly contests the motion's central claim that Orthodox theism supplies a necessary and effective ground or guarantor for logical laws.
Jay Dyer's claim that God necessarily grounds and guarantees the laws of logic.
After discussing shared language and communication, Matt turns to whether a divine guarantor is necessary and presents a dilemma about God's relation to logic.
Even a perfect divine foundation cannot give flawed human minds maximal epistemic warrant unless God removes their fallibility altogether.
The argument separates an allegedly perfect metaphysical ground from human access to knowledge, challenging the claimed epistemic benefit of theism.
Jay Dyer's contention that a perfect God can ground knowledge and provide epistemic certainty.
Matt shifts from God's relation to logical laws to the believer's fallible cognitive access, using the image of clean water passing through a dirty filter.
If logical laws could not have been otherwise, positing an additional entity to guarantee their necessity is unnecessary and absurd.
This is a direct alternative to the transcendental conclusion: logical necessity may be primitive and therefore need no theistic foundation whatsoever.
Jay Dyer's assertion that necessary logical truths require God as their explanatory guarantee.
At the end of Matt's formal segment, he proposes that logic may simply be necessarily true and argues that a guarantor adds nothing to that necessity.
Matt's worldview, consistently followed, leads to solipsism or total skepticism while still relying on categories that its presuppositions cannot support.
This states Jay's central transcendental strategy: expose the opponent's continued reliance on intelligibility while arguing that his worldview cannot account for it.
Matt Dillahunty's fallibilist worldview and his claim that uncertainty does not prevent warranted reasoning.
Beginning the conversational exchange, Jay dismisses psychological motives as irrelevant to truth and argues that Matt does not follow his skeptical premises consistently.
Fallible skepticism permits reasonable confidence in logic, while Jay still must demonstrate that logic requires any foundation beyond its observed reliability.
Matt rejects the alleged slide from fallibilism to global skepticism and returns the burden to the proposition that logic needs a transcendent foundation.
Jay Dyer's argument that Matt's skeptical commitments consistently entail solipsism or total skepticism.
Matt distinguishes skepticism from cynicism, describes confidence as proportional rather than absolute, and asks what demonstrates a need for something beyond logic.
Appealing to induction because it pragmatically works is circular and does not supply the logical justification that an atheistic worldview requires.
Induction is one of the motion's named domains, and Jay uses its alleged circularity to argue that Matt relies on an unjustified transcendental precondition.
Matt Dillahunty's appeal to induction's continued practical reliability as grounds for reasonable confidence.
After Matt says both participants rely on logic, Jay presses induction as a test case and argues that judging it true because it works presupposes its reliability.
Divine providence explains nature's regularity and the possibility of science, logic, and mathematics, whereas sense experience and pragmatism alone do not.
The move supplies Jay's affirmative explanatory account for induction and intelligibility rather than merely criticizing the skeptical alternative for inconsistency.
Matt Dillahunty's position that no need for a further explanation or foundation has been demonstrated.
Jay argues that asking meta-level explanatory questions is legitimate, then presents providence as the reason nature is regular enough for rational and scientific practices.
A current explanatory dead end does not validate the theistic branch of a reductio unless the need for an explanation is first demonstrated.
This attacks the inference form of the transcendental argument, arguing that failure to supply a non-theistic explanation does not establish God as necessary.
Jay Dyer's claim that lacking a non-theistic explanation leaves the theistic explanation as the required conclusion.
Following disagreement about whether Matt predicted a future answer, Matt reconstructs Jay's argument and explains why an unresolved branch does not prove its alternative.
The transcendental argument is a positive holistic case: the theistic worldview coherently accounts for necessary transcendental categories and their interrelations.
This clarifies the affirmative case at the heart of the debate by denying that TAG merely finds defects in an opponent and infers theism by default.
Matt Dillahunty's reconstruction of Jay's case as an invalid inference from a non-theistic explanatory dead end.
After discussing skeptical and epistemological traditions, Jay says TAG positively integrates metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, and other necessary preconditions into one coherent system.
Accepting logic provisionally is not denying logic or asserting that it lacks a foundation; the unsupported claim is that a foundation, specifically God, is required.
The distinction blocks Jay's consequence-based critique and locates the burden on the affirmative claim that logical absolutes need and receive a divine foundation.
Jay Dyer's argument that denying or failing to justify fundamental logical presuppositions destroys rational discourse.
Matt calls the appeal to consequences irrelevant, affirms practical reliance on logic, distinguishes nonbelief from contrary belief, and notes that Jay also accepts something ungrounded.
Because induction undergirds science but cannot itself be logically justified through empiricism, the transcendental argument is the appropriate next explanatory step.
This directly connects the alleged inability of empiricism to justify induction with the debate's central claim that a transcendental theistic ground is necessary.
Matt's account of induction as a reliable but approximate basis for scientific inference.
After Matt characterizes induction as probabilistic inference supported by experience, Jay accepts that practical description but argues that it leaves the belief in induction logically unjustified.
A fundamental incoherence between epistemology and metaphysics would devastate a worldview, while the transcendental argument supplies the needed coherent justification.
The move explains the claimed consequence of an ungrounded epistemology and presents transcendental theism as the account that prevents systemic worldview collapse.
Matt's position that discovering a missing foundation would revise rather than crush his worldview.

Responding to the question about epistemic breakdown, Jay argues that failures involving logic or the external world are foundational, that all systems terminate in an ultimate authority, and that transcendental reasoning is valid.
Not knowing whether logical absolutes require a foundation does not assert that they require none, and their demonstrated practical reliability permits their use without a causal explanation.
This challenges the argument's burden-shifting premise by separating justified use of logic from knowledge of its ultimate ground and rejecting God as a required explanation.
Jay's claim that Matt says logical absolutes need no justification and cannot coherently use them without one.
Matt denies claiming that logic has no needed foundation, accepts that its reliability and truth are presupposed, and argues that knowing a system works does not require knowing how or why it works.
Skepticism properly permits an answer of uncertainty, and discomfort with uncertainty encourages fallacious explanatory leaps rather than genuine knowledge.
It defends the legitimacy of epistemic suspension against the demand for a transcendental ground and argues that invoking God does not increase explanatory understanding.
Jay's contention that a skeptic should justify the reliability of logic rather than answer that he does not know.

Matt says uncertainty can be the correct skeptical response, warns that dissatisfaction with it motivates logical errors, and characterizes the theistic answer as an unexplained appeal to divine authority.
Atheism cannot consistently employ immaterial transcendental categories such as truth and logic while declining to justify their reality, whereas theism accounts for their use.
This states the core internal-critique form of Jay's case: the opponent allegedly relies on categories that the atheistic worldview cannot justify but the theistic worldview can.
Matt's characterization of the transcendental appeal to God as an unsatisfying assertion without explanatory value.
Jay responds that everyone relies on immaterial categories, contends that Matt cannot establish truth as real on atheism, and treats this reliance as evidence that atheism is false.
Atheism need not assert universal divine nonexistence; the rational position can be nonbelief, while particular god concepts may be rejected when they conflict with observation.
The distinction determines what burden the skeptical side bears and blocks attempts to treat nonbelief as a metaphysical assertion requiring proof of universal nonexistence.
The audience question framing Matt as holding the positive belief that God does not exist.

Matt rejects the question's framing, explains that god claims must be defined individually, allows confident rejection of observationally contradictory gods, and identifies his general position as lack of conviction.
Skeptical neutrality is unavailable at the paradigmatic level because even suspended judgment entails logical, metaphysical, and justificatory commitments.
This attempts to defeat the con side's burden-of-proof defense by arguing that nonbelief itself depends upon worldview-level commitments subject to transcendental evaluation.
Matt's distinction between lacking belief in God and positively believing that no God exists.

Jay argues that neutrality still carries metaphysical implications, responds to Matt's wallet counterexample by separating ordinary claims from paradigm-level preconditions, and stresses the foundational significance of logic.
Logical principles describe invariant relations but need not exist as independent prescriptive entities, so their practical and conceptual status does not establish a divine ontology.
The account offers a direct alternative to the proposed theistic grounding of logic by treating logical laws as descriptions of how reality is rather than divine entities.
The challenge that Matt cannot affirm logic's ontological status without identifying its ultimate ground.
Matt says mind-independent reality would still exhibit the relations described by logic, while denying that logical laws must exist as separate prescriptive objects with an ontology of their own.
Transcendental arguments compare paradigms and address unique preconditions at a meta-logical level, so ordinary objections to conventional arguments do not dispose of them.
This defends the methodological legitimacy of the central transcendental case and explains why Jay believes conventional evidentiary criticism fails to engage its distinctive structure.
Matt's claim that Jay has supplied assertions rather than evidence warranting the conclusion that God exists.
Jay describes the argument as a comparison of two paradigms concerning transcendental preconditions, appeals to analogous reasoning in mathematics, and rejects dismissal of the form as unjustifiable.
Without a sufficiently explicit argument structure, soundness and validity cannot be assessed, and calling a claim meta-logical does not remove the need for clear premises and inferential form.
This targets whether the pro side has presented an assessable argument at all, making explicit structure a prerequisite for establishing either validity or soundness.
Jay's defense of transcendental arguments as valid meta-level reasoning used across multiple disciplines.

Matt distinguishes validity from soundness, argues that conversational shorthand can obscure invalid structure, and explains why formal premises are needed to evaluate a proposition or conduct a reductio.
Human access to truth does not require claiming absolute certainty or pretending that ultimate skeptical problems have been solved.
This directly supplies the skeptical alternative to the proposed theistic grounding of truth and knowledge by distinguishing practical epistemic confidence from absolute certainty.
The earlier claim that transcendental categories can be justified because they ultimately point to God.
After Jay argues that causality and other transcendental categories receive justification through God, Matt explains his fallibilist approach to truth and unresolved skeptical questions.
Logic is unavoidable in reasoning, while practical concern for truth and survival provides reasons to remain logically consistent without a theistic foundation.
The move presents a direct nontheistic account of why logical norms are indispensable and worth following, addressing a principal grounding claim in the motion.
The challenge that Matt's recommendation to follow logic is an ethical claim his worldview cannot ground.
A questioner characterizes adherence to logic as a metaethical obligation; Matt distinguishes unavoidable logical presupposition from practical reasons for valuing consistency and truth.
Standards of sufficient evidence vary by claim, and belief occurs when an individual is actually convinced rather than when a universal evidentiary threshold is crossed.
This establishes Matt's claim-relative evidential epistemology as an alternative to Jay's proposed universal transcendental warrant for knowledge and justified belief.
In response to a neutral question about when demonstration becomes convincing, Matt explains proportional evidence, individual conviction, cognitive bias, and divergent standards of warrant.
Both parties presuppose the same transcendental categories, but Orthodox theism uniquely explains them through God as the metaphysical answer to meta-level questions.
This is a concise statement of the affirmative case: shared logical and epistemic preconditions allegedly receive their ultimate justification from the metaphysical reality of God.
Matt's objection that Jay additionally presupposes God and therefore does not share only the same presuppositions.
Asked which participant makes more presuppositions, the exchange turns to whether God is an additional unsupported assumption or the solution to shared meta-level categories.
Once a belief has an explanatory or evidentiary foundation, it is derived from that foundation rather than merely presupposed.
The distinction challenges the affirmative's terminology and pressures Jay to clarify whether logic is unsupportedly assumed or genuinely derived from a demonstrated divine foundation.
Jay's claim that transcendental categories may be presupposed while also receiving logical justification through God.
After Jay says shared categories are both real and logically justified, Matt argues that justification changes their status from presuppositions into conclusions derived from evidence.
Transcendental categories can receive positive proof because their denial necessarily assumes them, even though that proof differs from ordinary empirical demonstration.
This supplies the core inferential mechanism for the affirmative case by explaining how necessary preconditions may be demonstrated without being treated as ordinary empirical objects.
Matt's contention that a presupposition with evidentiary warrant ceases to be a presupposition at all.
Following disagreement over the meaning of presupposition, Jay distinguishes modes of proof and develops the denial-dependent form of transcendental justification through a historical example.
Logical laws are neither independently imposed on God nor arbitrarily changeable by God, but reflect the divine mind within the Orthodox worldview.
The move addresses the central divine-command-style dilemma for logical grounding and explains how the affirmative relates necessity, omnipotence, and the nature of God.
The dilemma asking whether God generates the laws of logic or instead must obey laws independent of God.
A question poses whether God creates or submits to logic; Jay rejects both alternatives and identifies logical truth with reflections of the divine mind.
Without God, knowledge understood as justified true belief or a coherent account of beliefs becomes impossible and ultimately collapses into absurdity.
This states the affirmative's ultimate conclusion about epistemic dependence on God and directly connects the transcendental argument to the impossibility of knowledge otherwise.
Near the debate's conclusion, Jay answers a direct question about whether knowledge is possible without God and presents the result as a summary of his argument.
A divine guarantee of logic may be psychologically satisfying, but it is an unnecessary additional step unless its necessity is actually demonstrated.
This directly contests the modal burden of the affirmative case: agreement about logic's reliability does not itself establish that God is needed to explain or guarantee it.
Jay's central claim that God is necessary to ground and guarantee the absolute, invariant character of logic.
In closing remarks, Matt acknowledges why belief in a divine guarantor can reassure people while denying that the debate established such a guarantor as necessary.
Properly basic beliefs do not stop foundationalism's regress or circularity, whereas a coherentist account better explains relations among beliefs and truth.
The move rejects a major rival solution to ultimate epistemic justification and locates Jay's transcendental approach within a coherentist critique of classical foundationalism.
Asked about properly basic beliefs, Jay argues that simply declaring beliefs basic restates foundational circularity and uses the Cartesian project to motivate a coherentist alternative.
Orthodox theology treats logical laws as descriptions of God's energies or actions, not as descriptions of the inaccessible divine essence.
This directly specifies how the pro side claims Orthodox theism grounds logic while avoiding the objection that logic merely redescribes God's nature.
The preceding question argues that making logic descriptive of God's logical nature fails to explain why God is logical.
A submitted question challenges the explanatory value of grounding logic in God's nature, and Dyer answers through the distinctively Orthodox essence-energy framework.
God is self-evident in one qualified sense, but is not self-evident in the sense presupposed by classical foundationalism.
The qualification bears directly on the pro side's epistemology by distinguishing its claimed basis for God from classical foundationalist self-evidence.
The submitted question asks whether God should be regarded as self-evident.
Near the end of audience questions, Dyer gives a concise clarification of how his position can affirm one notion of self-evidence while rejecting another.
Correct moral conclusions can be reached through entirely secular means, making claims that secularism necessarily produces atrocities an unsupported reversal.
The account advances the con side's core position that theistic foundations are unnecessary for moral knowledge and challenges an asserted consequence of secularism.

While discussing possible future conversations about Orthodox theology, Dillahunty recalls a morality debate in which an Orthodox opponent accepted secular moral reasoning before condemning secularism.
Historical prophecy may be strong evidence, but its force depends on governing presuppositions that determine whether prophecy is possible and how evidence is interpreted.
The answer restates the pro side's central transcendental thesis that evidence cannot function independently of the worldview-level presuppositions governing interpretation.
The audience question asks whether historically confirmed prophecy can exceed the mere internal coherence and circularity shared by worldviews.
Dyer grants that biblical prophecy can supply a strong argument, illustrates the claim with Daniel, and then subordinates evidential judgments to deeper presuppositional commitments.
Openness to prophecy is necessary but insufficient for justified belief, because competing prophecies still require evidence that their alleged predictive ability is genuine.
The reply challenges the pro side's account of evidence by distinguishing prior openness from adequate demonstration and highlighting rival purported prophetic sources.
Dyer argues that prophecy will not persuade anyone unless governing presuppositions first permit prophecy and shape its evidential interpretation.
Dillahunty accepts that a person must allow prophecy to be possible, but argues that this does not validate a particular prophecy or remove the need for discriminating evidence.
